tutorials.title: 1. Hello in Terminal
tutorials.summary: Print your first message and find stdout without searching through panels.
tutorials.observe: Build & load, then Run. Open Terminal: the message must appear there, followed by exit status 0. Building alone does not run the program.
tutorials.experiment: Change the greeting, rebuild and run. Save the workspace to keep the source and execution history together.

tutorials.title: 2. Input with scanf
tutorials.summary: Read a name and number interactively; understand waiting for input and EOF.
tutorials.observe: Run. At each prompt, type an answer in the field below Terminal output and press Enter. For the reference result, send Ada, then 7. Enter submits a line; Send EOF ends the input stream.
tutorials.experiment: Reset and send EOF at the first prompt. Then reset and try Ada followed by abc: the program reports the invalid integer. The input widths bound the name and number.
tutorials.output: Your name: Years of experience (0-999): Hello, Ada! Next year: 8.

tutorials.title: 3. Understand and undo a change
tutorials.summary: Connect C assignments, Assembly instructions, registers and RAM.
tutorials.observe: Build & load. In Symbols, double-click result to reveal its address in Memory. Step through the stores, use Back, then Replay forward. The same bytes must return.
tutorials.experiment: Set a breakpoint by double-clicking an Assembly instruction. Run to it, inspect the state, then continue. Try optimization 2 and compare the instruction sequence.

tutorials.title: 4. Write Assembly directly
tutorials.summary: An Assembly entry point prints a message without C startup or a C library.
tutorials.observe: Follow t0, t1, a0 and a7 in Registers. The loop writes one byte at a time with service 0x100; service 93 exits. These services are defined by the Teaching environment and are not Linux system calls.
tutorials.experiment: Change the text. The label difference calculates its new byte count automatically. Step through la to see how the assembler expands a pseudo-instruction.

tutorials.title: 5. C and Assembly together
tutorials.summary: A C function delegates an addition to a RISC-V instruction.
tutorials.observe: Use optimization 0 and start the C debugger. Step into add_on_cpu, inspect its arguments and step over the add instruction. The constraints let the compiler choose registers safely.
tutorials.experiment: Change the input globals and the expected result together. For a separate .S file, add a source file to the project and mark it for compilation.

tutorials.title: 6. Work with virtual files
tutorials.summary: Create, read and inspect a file in simulated RAM.
tutorials.observe: Run to completion and open Program files. Select result.txt to read its bytes. Save file exports a copy to a location you choose on the notebook.
tutorials.experiment: Change the text and rebuild. Save the workspace, reopen it and inspect the same virtual file. The program cannot silently overwrite a host file through fopen.

tutorials.title: 7. Draw from RAM
tutorials.summary: Draw a diagonal line and connect pixels to stores in memory.
tutorials.observe: Build & load, open Graphical display and run. A 64 by 32 monochrome display shows a diagonal. Each pixel comes from the pixels array in simulated RAM.
tutorials.experiment: Step through the loop and use Back/Replay to remove and restore pixels. Detach the display panel with its title-bar menu and restore the layout through View.

tutorials.title: 8. C17 threads and atomics
tutorials.summary: Two harts cooperate through a C17 thread and a shared atomic counter.
tutorials.observe: Hosted threads starts main once. Run with all harts scheduled; select each hart to inspect its registers. Joining the thread ensures that all 200 increments finish before printing.
tutorials.experiment: Change each loop limit to 200 and update the expected total. Deterministic interleaving helps reproduce a run; it does not explore every weak-memory execution.

tutorials.title: 9. Follow an LR/SC reservation
tutorials.summary: Inspect atomic add, load-reserved and store-conditional as instructions.
tutorials.observe: Step through LR and SC in Assembly. Inspect the shared counter in Memory. SC reports zero on success; the final counter is 43.
tutorials.experiment: Pause between LR and SC and edit the reserved bytes in Memory. The edit cancels the reservation, so SC fails. Reset before comparing the reference result again.

tutorials.title: 10. Floating point and exact bits
tutorials.summary: Compare a double value with its binary64 encoding and rounding flags.
tutorials.observe: Run and open Floating point and CSRs. Follow the fused multiply-add and compare its decimal result with the exact register bits.
tutorials.experiment: Try inputs that are not exact binary fractions, such as 0.1 and 0.2. Rebuild and inspect the flags. The original reference result applies to the original source.

tutorials.title: 11. Four elements in one vector
tutorials.summary: Load four elements, add ten in parallel and store the vector.
tutorials.observe: Step through vsetvli, vle32.v, vadd.vi and vse32.v in Assembly. Open Vectors and CSRs to inspect v8, v9, vl and vtype. The reference result is [11, 12, 13, 14].
tutorials.experiment: Change the immediate ten to another value and update the reference checks in C. Back/Replay restores vector registers and stored elements together.

tutorials.title: 12. Handle timer interrupts
tutorials.summary: A firmware handler receives three simulated timer interrupts and returns with mret.
tutorials.observe: The Firmware environment enables machine trap handling. Step through the handler and inspect mepc, mcause and mstatus in CSRs. The timer advances with simulated instruction progress.
tutorials.experiment: Use Back across an interrupt entry to restore the interrupted context. Change the timer interval to compare instruction progress, without interpreting it as physical timing.
